name: citor
workload: Recursive fork-join benchmarks (skynet 100M tasks, nqueens, fib(39), matmul 2048) run by the independent tzcnt/runtime-benchmarks suite with 64 worker threads.
claimed_speedup: Suite summary table (64 cores): mean ratio to best 1.06x for citor vs 3.25x for tbb; skynet 24932 us vs tbb 142887 us; fib(39) 49966 us vs tbb 215592 us; nqueens 80765 us vs tbb 125730 us; matmul(2048) 48069 us vs tbb 50127 us.
hardware: EPYC 7742 64-core, 64 worker threads (no SMT), Debian 13, boost enabled / schedutil governor
tradeoffs: Header-only C++20, Linux x86_64 and Windows x86_64 validated. Design target is single-CCD Zen with physical-core pinning; topology detection does not model multi-socket EPYC, hybrid cores or Intel mesh yet. Chase-Lev work stealing plus per-CCD arenas; coroutine frames are heap allocated.
caveats: The suite is maintained by the author of a competing runtime (TooManyCooks) and citor is a very young project, so the table moves with revisions (citor's README says it topped the summary as of May 2026). The README itself admits losses: stencil/barrier-bound workloads lose to OpenMP on multi-CCD, heavy-tailed reductions lose to oneTBB (static partitioning), and on larger hosts it loses recursive fork-join to libfork unless PoolGroup is used. The suite only covers four recursive workloads. matmul margin vs tbb is small (about 4 percent). OpenMP and Rayon are not in the suite; citor's own README benchmark compares to OpenMP, oneTBB, Taskflow, BS, dispenso and others on Zen 5 with charts only (numbers not tabulated).
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'fork-join runtime benchmark Fibonacci nqueens Cilk oneTBB Taskflow OpenMP comparison C++ new scheduler github' surfaced tzcnt/runtime-benchmarks and citor

name: ForkUnion (Fork Union)
workload: N-body (512 bodies, microseconds per parallel-for dispatch) and connected components by label propagation (84 fork-join rounds on a ~27M-edge graph, GTEPS), run on every logical core vs OpenMP, Rayon and Taskflow.
claimed_speedup: README: 'often ~3-6x faster than OpenMP and ~12-16x faster than Rayon and Taskflow' per parallel-for dispatch. N-body table, 128x Intel SPR Linux (static/dynamic, us): ForkUnion C++ 54/86, OpenMP 115/226, Rayon 483/739, Taskflow 666/694. Connected components 128x SPR (GTEPS): ForkUnion C++ 46.5/20.9, OpenMP 28.2/0.4, Rayon 8.5/6.5, Taskflow 25.1/0.5.
compiler_and_flags: identical -O3 and -march=native / target-cpu=native on all sides, no LTO; compiler versions not stated on the page
hardware: Machines named only as '18x Apple M5 Pro', '24x Intel RPL, Windows', '128x Intel SPR, Linux', '192x AWS Graviton 5, Linux'; exact CPU SKUs not given
stars_or_usage: 379 stars; used in USearch, NumKong, StringZilla
tradeoffs: Not a task-queue: deliberately bans nested parallelism, futures, task graphs, async work and work that outlives its scope. Fork-join only, with NUMA pinning and optional hardware address-monitor waits (UMWAIT/WFET). C, C++, Rust and Zig APIs.
caveats: First-party benchmark with public scripts (scripts/nbody.*, scripts/propagation.*) but exact CPU model and compiler version missing, so tier C. Dispatch-latency microbenchmark, not a general workload; OpenMP is on equal footing for loops but the dynamic OpenMP column collapses to 0.4 GTEPS on SPR and Graviton. On the 24x Intel RPL Windows box OpenMP static wins connected components (11.4 vs 10.0) and the Rust build wins several cells. Earlier blog post (ashvardanian.com, blocked here) and ParallelReductionsBenchmark README report 467.7 MB/s vs OpenMP 585.5 MB/s vs Taskflow 76.3 MB/s for parallel reductions on Graviton (OpenMP still ahead there). Baseline is OpenMP not TBB; oneTBB is not benchmarked.

name: Scheduling (dpuyda)
workload: Recursive async Fibonacci (n up to 35) and a linear chain task graph (up to 2M tasks) timed with Google Benchmark, versus Taskflow examples; matmul 2048 comparable.
claimed_speedup: README Google Benchmark output: fibonacci/35 wall 1661 ms (Scheduling) vs 15058 ms (Taskflow); linear_chain/33554432 wall 4158 ms vs 9951 ms; linear_chain/2097152 250 ms vs 496 ms. 9.1x and 2.4x (derived from page data).
hardware: Intel i7-1165G7 (README mislabels as Xeon) @ 2.80GHz, 32 CPUs per Google Benchmark header
tradeoffs: Header-only C++20, small API (ThreadPool, task graphs, Chase-Lev deque). No TBB/OpenMP/Rayon comparison.
caveats: Baseline is Taskflow, not TBB/OpenMP/Rayon, so baseline_in_list is false. Compiler and flags not stated in what I read; first-party and arXiv preprint (not confirmed peer reviewed). Hardware string reads 32 CPUs on a laptop-class i7-1165G7, which looks wrong.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch result for arXiv 2407.15805 'A simple and fast C++ thread pool implementation capable of running task graphs'
